name: Spaghetti Squash Boats with Chicken
writer_notes: Each of the 7 squash is halved into 2 boats, giving 14 boats = 14 servings = one boat per container. Portioning is one boat per serving; only the filling needs to be divided evenly.

Olive oil, the 1 3/4 tsp salt portion, and black pepper are folded into step 1 (the roast) because the source roasts the squash 'according to' a separate linked Roasted Spaghetti Squash recipe; keeping them there prevents orphaned ingredients. The scant 1 tsp salt and pepper season the chicken in step 3.

FLAG for repair pass: black pepper appears under-scaled. Source seasons pepper twice at 1/4 tsp (squash + chicken) = 1/2 tsp, which at 3.5x should be 1 3/4 tsp, and salt kept exactly that two-portion shape. The locked view shows only one pepper line, scant 1 tsp (~the chicken portion alone). Confirm whether the squash pepper portion was dropped.
Source step 7 typo 'until the cheesy is bubbly' rendered as 'cheese is bubbly'.

No cost_lines or cost_ps were supplied in this dispatch, so shop_smart deliberately avoids any per-ounce, per-package, or 'lasts N batches' claim. Only money in prose is the ${{cost_ps}} token and the $1/month membership line.
Macros used only from the locked view: 475 cal and 40.5 g protein per serving. All in band (cal 450-700, carbs <=40 at 36, protein >=40 at 40.5).
intro_html:
Here is a trick your grocery budget will thank you for: turn a squash into the bowl. Spaghetti squash roasts down into tender strands that catch a warm filling the way pasta never quite does, and each half becomes its own container. No noodles to boil, no extra dish to wash, and the vegetable is doing the work of both the side and the plate.

Inside these boats is the good stuff. Crisp bacon for smoke, seared chicken breast for the protein that keeps you full, wilted spinach, a spoon of Greek yogurt to make it creamy without a heavy cream bill, and part-skim mozzarella melted over the top. It lands at 475 calories and 40 grams of protein a serving, and it tastes like something you would happily pay restaurant prices for. Not bad for a dinner built around a cheap vegetable.
ingredients_display: Spaghetti Squash: 7 medium spaghetti squash, about 2 lb each, halved lengthwise and seeded (6350 g)
Olive Oil: 2 1/3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil (32 g)
Salt (Morton): 1 3/4 tsp kosher salt; scant 1 tsp kosher salt (15 g)
Black Pepper (Great Value): scant 1 tsp ground black pepper (4 g)
Hickory Smoked Bacon (Great Value): 14 strips thick-sliced center-cut bacon, roughly chopped (168 g)
Boneless Skinless Chicken Breast (Member's Mark): 3 1/2 lb boneless skinless chicken breasts, cut into bite-sized pieces (1588 g)
Spinach: 7 cups baby spinach, torn into pieces (210 g)
Plain Yogurt (generic (USDA)): 1 3/4 cups nonfat plain Greek yogurt (427 g)
Mozzarella Cheese (generic (USDA)): 3 1/2 cups shredded part-skim mozzarella cheese, divided (396 g)
Fresh Basil: 7 tbsp chopped fresh basil, plus more for serving (10 g)

Add it up and this comes out to ${{cost_ps}} a serving for a dinner that eats like a restaurant plate: real chicken, bacon, and melted cheese sitting in its own roasted squash bowl. That is the whole pitch of cooking this way. You buy in batch sizes, you let a cheap vegetable carry the plate, and you stop paying takeout prices for something you can make better at home.

shop_smart:
• Buy the spaghetti squash whole and firm, with a hard rind and no soft spots. This batch calls for seven of them at roughly two pounds each, so pick them up over a couple of store trips if your cart runs out of room. They keep for weeks on the counter, so buying ahead is fine.
  • Boneless skinless chicken breast is the anchor here at three and a half pounds. Buy the largest family pack your store stocks rather than the small tray, and cut it into bite-sized pieces yourself at home.
  • Thick-sliced center-cut bacon is worth asking for by name. Center-cut gives you more meat and less fringe fat, and you only need the crisp bits and about a tablespoon of the rendered fat to cook the chicken in, so a single package carries the whole batch.
  • Grab nonfat plain Greek yogurt, not flavored and not regular. It brings the creamy body without the sugar, and the plain tub pulls double duty in dressings and breakfasts the rest of the week.
  • Baby spinach wilts down to almost nothing, so the seven cups here is one clamshell, not a wheelbarrow. Buy fresh basil as a small bunch and save a little to sprinkle at serving.
make_it:
Set an oven rack in the center and heat the oven to 400 degrees. Halve the spaghetti squash lengthwise, scoop the seeds, and rub the cut faces with the olive oil, then season with kosher salt and black pepper. Roast the halves until the flesh is tender and pulls into strands. Take them out to cool and drop the oven to 350 degrees.

While the squash roasts, heat a large saucepan over medium and add the chopped bacon. Cook until it is crisp and the fat has rendered, about 8 minutes, then lift the bacon out with a slotted spoon onto a paper towel lined plate and pat it dry. Pour off all but about a tablespoon of that bacon fat and turn the heat up to medium-high.

Add the chicken pieces to the pan and season with the garlic powder, salt, and pepper. Saute until the chicken is cooked through, about 5 minutes. Pull the pan off the heat and stir in the spinach until it wilts, then fold in the Greek yogurt, half of the mozzarella, and the chopped basil so it all comes together creamy.

Once the squash is cool enough to handle, run a fork through the inside to shred and fluff the strands until they pull away from the walls and make a nest. Divide the chicken filling evenly among the boats, lightly mixing it into the squash with the fork. Set the stuffed boats on a baking sheet, scatter the reserved bacon and the remaining mozzarella over the top, and bake at 350 until the cheese is bubbly, about 10 minutes. Let them cool a few minutes, then serve hot with a little extra basil.
portion_html:
This one portions itself, which is the beauty of it. Seven squash halved gives you 14 boats, and each boat is one serving in one container. No scale needed, no fighting over who got the bigger scoop.

The only place to be even-handed is the filling. Split the chicken mixture across all 14 nests evenly before you top and bake, so every container lands near the same 475 calories and 40 grams of protein. Let the boats cool before you lid them, and they stack neatly in the fridge for the week.
credit_html: Recipe adapted from wellplated.com, rebuilt for 14-serving budget meal prep with weighed portions and Omaha pricing.
upsell_html: Make it once and you will see why the boat beats the bowl. Same warm, cheesy, high-protein dinner, none of the noodle bill, and cleanup is basically the baking sheet. Pack the 14 containers, stack them in the fridge, and let future you thank present you every night this week.
